sample.unit_of_observation: individual-year (person-year); individual-month for the take-up and monthly earnings analysis from 2008
selection_rules: + Fully eligible for student benefits (eligible for benefits the entire year, excluding e.g. those who start their education in September or finish during the year, and periods of paid internships): 94,700 (7.9%)
+ Positive labor earnings, defined as earned income above DKK 8000 per year = core sample: 75,500 (6.3%)
sample.period: 2006-2011 (average sample sizes reported for 2006-2011; the student benefit system is described as largely unchanged over 2004-2011; monthly earnings and hours data available from 2008; Table 3 and Table 4 use 2008)
sample.n_observations: around 75,000 observations per year; Table 2 reports an average core sample of 75,500 individuals per year, 2006-2011. Table 4 uses 16,743 observations.

construction_notes: All monetary amounts in the paper have been scaled to 2018-levels using the official (wage) indexation of the student benefits; DKK 6.4 is approximately USD 1 at 2018 exchange rates.

Income counted against the income limit includes labor income (net of labor market contribution), transfers other than student benefits and capital income with the exception of certain types of stock income.

The basic benefit rate for the typical student in tertiary education is DKK 6100 per month; the baseline income limit before 2009 is DKK 7700 per month (12 x 7700 per year); each month of benefits not taken up raises the income limit by DKK 11,600, a phase-out rate of 6100/11,600 = 52%.

The 2009 reform raised the baseline income limit by 24% on top of regular wage indexation, corresponding to DKK 21,900, and raised the phase-out rate from 52 to 62%, raising the effective marginal tax rate from 72 to 78%.

Individual marginal tax and phase-out rates are not observed; the author develops a simulation model (similar to NBER TAXSIM) of individual phase-out rates, distance to the income limits and payback of student benefits. The model predicts individual student benefits within DKK +/- 2 for 98% of the core sample (online Appendix C).

The optimal region for individuals taking up less than full benefits is excess income between DKK 0 and 11,600; the dominated region is excess income above DKK 11,600, where the effective marginal tax rate is 100%.
Table 4 controls non-parametrically for earned income in bins of DKK 4000 and uses robust standard errors.

Study related jobs are defined as all jobs not in wholesale (NACE 46), retail (NACE 47), postal service (NACE 53), hotels and restaurants (NACE 55, 56), cleaning (NACE 81), elderly, social and childcare (NACE 87, 88) and sports and amusement facilities (NACE 93).
'No. of past years in tertiary education' is the number of years in tertiary education over the last four years.

Predicted excess income for month m: realized earnings up to and including month m plus predicted rest-of-year earnings assuming monthly earnings stay constant at the average of months m and m-1, minus the individual income limit implied by observed take-up up to month m and full take-up thereafter.
